project.topic: What if a rogue planet passed between Earth and Mars?
project.title: What if a Rogue Planet Passed Between Earth and Mars? Goodbye, Moon
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If a rogue planet as heavy as Jupiter flew between Earth and Mars and missed us, what would its gravity still do to us?
project.viewer_takeaway: A near miss is enough: a Jupiter-mass rogue passing 3.5 million km away would raise huge tides, could pull the Moon out of Earth orbit and would leave Earth on a stretched orbit with longer, darker northern winters.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Earth orbits the Sun at 1 AU with eccentricity 0.0167 (perihelion in early January) and the Moon orbits Earth at 384,400 km; the nearest planet, Mars, orbits at 1.52 AU with eccentricity 0.093. Rogue (free-floating) planets exist in our galaxy; Jupiter-mass ones appear rarer than about one per star.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: A rogue gas giant with Jupiter's mass and size falls in from interstellar space (26 km/s far from the Sun, like the interstellar object Oumuamua) on a prograde path in Earth's orbital plane, with its closest point to the Sun 1.026 AU, between the orbits of Earth and Mars. It passes Earth at 3.47 million km (9 Moon distances) in late September, overtaking Earth from behind on the outside; the Moon is near full, on the side facing the rogue.
assumptions: Rogue: 1 Jupiter mass, Jupiter-like radius and cloud albedo; no moons of its own.
Geometry chosen for the strongest defensible near miss: prograde, coplanar, closest approach in late September with the Moon near full; other geometries give smaller effects.

Orbital outcomes come from a four-body (Sun, Earth, Moon, rogue) numerical integration of this geometry. Mars sits about 75 million km beyond the rogue at closest approach (near opposition), so the rogue literally passes between the two planets; Mars is only slightly nudged and its change is not modelled.
The harbour town (50 N, east-facing coast), its tide range and the people, cars and boats shown are illustrative.
Climate changes after the pass are described only through sunlight and season length.
causal_chain: The rogue is lit by our Sun, so it rises at dusk as a banded disc 2.2-2.4 degrees wide, far brighter than the full Moon.
Its tidal pull on Earth peaks at about 35 times the Moon's (about 30 times on the night shown), so coastal water drains while it is near the horizon and floods while it is high.
For about 3.5 days its gravity on Earth exceeds the Sun's; Earth and the Moon are pulled unequally.
In this geometry the Moon gains enough speed relative to Earth to escape; it drifts away and shrinks to a star-like point within about two months, then orbits the Sun on its own.
Earth itself receives a 3.9 km/s kick: its orbit becomes as eccentric as Mars's (0.091), its year lengthens by about 18 days and aphelion moves to early January.
With aphelion in northern winter, the northern winter half-year lasts about 35 days longer than today and January sunlight is about 24% weaker.
uncertainties: Whether the Moon escapes depends on its position during the pass: in the integration it escapes for about 40% of lunar positions at this distance and is left on a badly stretched orbit otherwise.
Real coastal tide heights depend on basin resonance, friction and how quickly the forcing ramps; the 9 m harbour range shown is illustrative.
The size of the climate response (snow, sea ice, ice-sheet growth) to the new orbit is not modelled.
A slower, closer or more massive rogue would do more; a faster or more distant one much less.
Effects in the Southern Hemisphere are the reverse of those shown: milder, shorter winters and hotter summers.

claims.statement: Rogue planets that drift without a star exist; Jupiter-mass ones appear rarer than about one per star.
claims.reasoning: NASA describes rogue planets found by microlensing and expected from the Roman telescope; Mroz et al. (2017) set an upper limit near 0.25 Jupiter-mass free-floating planets per star.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Present the visitor as a hypothetical rogue, not a known object or a prediction.

claims.statement: A Jupiter-size planet 3.5-3.7 million km away appears 2.2-2.4 degrees wide, about 4.5 Moon widths, and, lit by our Sun, outshines the full Moon many times over.
claims.reasoning: Angular size = 2 x 71,492 km / distance; Jupiter's geometric albedo 0.54 vs the Moon's 0.12 and about 17x the Moon's apparent area.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show it at true angular size; magnification only through the stated telephoto lenses.

claims.statement: At closest approach its tidal pull on Earth is about 35 times the Moon's; about 30 times on the night shown.
claims.reasoning: Tidal acceleration scales as mass / distance cubed: (1.898e27 / 7.346e22) x (384,400 / 3,470,000)^3 = 35; at 3.6 million km, about 31.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "thirty times harder"; compare forces, not tide heights.

claims.statement: Coastal water would drain far below normal while the rogue is near the horizon and rise metres above normal while it is high; the 9 m range shown is illustrative.
claims.reasoning: The equilibrium ocean tide scales with the forcing: about 0.5 m range for the Moon, so roughly 14 m in the open ocean at 30x; real coasts amplify or damp this.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Keep heights in the HUD as one harbour's readings; never claim a global number.

claims.statement: For about 3.5 days the rogue's gravity on Earth exceeds the Sun's.
claims.reasoning: GM/d^2: 8.6 mm/s^2 at 3.47 million km versus 5.9 mm/s^2 from the Sun at 1 AU; the integration gives 3.56 days above it.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Supporting fact for the reversal; not shown as a felt force (everything on Earth falls together).

claims.statement: In this geometry the Moon is pulled out of Earth orbit and ends up orbiting the Sun on its own (about 1.10 AU, eccentricity 0.11).
claims.reasoning: A four-body integration of the stated pass gives escape for Moon positions near full; the rogue's tidal pull at 9 Moon distances rivals Earth's hold on the Moon (Hill-sphere scale).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Keep the geometry note in the scope; do not claim every pass at this distance would take the Moon.

claims.statement: The escaping Moon recedes to about 1.1 million km after 10 nights and 4.3 million km after 60, shrinking from 0.47 to about 0.05 degrees: a bright star-like point.
claims.reasoning: Distances from the same integration; apparent size = 3,474 km / distance.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show nights explicitly in the HUD.

claims.statement: The pass changes Earth's orbit from eccentricity 0.017 to about 0.091, close to Mars's 0.093; the semimajor axis grows 3.3% and the year lengthens to about 384 days; aphelion reaches 1.13 AU.
claims.reasoning: Same integration: Earth gains about 3.9 km/s, mostly outward plus a forward drag from the faster rogue; passing bodies are known to reshape Earth's eccentricity (Kaib and Raymond 2024).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "as stretched as Mars's" and show the orbit, not a claim about Mars's climate.

claims.statement: With aphelion in early January, the northern winter half-year lasts about 214 days instead of 179 (about five weeks longer) and January sunlight is about 24% weaker than today.
claims.reasoning: Kepler timing on the new orbit between the equinox longitudes, and inverse-square sunlight at the January distance (1.128 AU) versus today's perihelion (0.983 AU).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Northern Hemisphere; the HUD says NORTHERN WINTER.

claims.statement: Longer winters with less sunlight would bring colder, snowier northern winters; the full climate response is uncertain.
claims.reasoning: Season length and seasonal sunlight drive surface temperature; NASA notes eccentricity sets season lengths and the perihelion-aphelion sunlight difference.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show one snowy harbour winter; do not quote global temperature numbers.

sources.name: NASA Science: Rogue Planets (Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope)
Mroz et al. 2017, No large population of unbound or wide-orbit Jupiter-mass planets
Kaib and Raymond 2024, Passing Stars as an Important Driver of Paleoclimate and the Solar System's Orbital Evolution (ApJL 962, L33)
NASA Science: Milankovitch (Orbital) Cycles and Their Role in Earth's Climate

creative_direction.logline: A starless planet as heavy as Jupiter threads the gap between Earth and Mars; it never touches us, but its gravity drains and floods your harbour, pulls the Moon away and leaves Earth on an orbit as stretched as Mars's.
creative_direction.visual_identity: A small stone harbour town at night lit by a giant banded planet: silver planet-light against warm sodium lamps, a telephoto planet-rise behind a lighthouse, a time-lapse flood, the Moon crossing the giant and shrinking night by night, a snowy January quay, then a clean glowing orbit map.
creative_direction.lighting: Night scenes keyed by cool silver planet-light from the rogue with warm practicals; long-lens sky shots exposed for the planet; winter scenes under a weak low sun and cold skylight; space under hard sunlight with a starfield.
creative_direction.camera_language: Eye-level handheld POV at the harbour (1.6 m) with telephoto lenses for the sky so true angular sizes read at phone size; one locked lighthouse framing reused for the planet-rise and the shrinking Moon; space shots pull back from Earth to a top-down orbit map.
creative_direction.motion_language: Time-lapse for tides and sky (HUD clock always visible), real time for people; a speed ramp into the overtopping; nights separated by brief dips; orbit lines draw progressively.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metres in the harbour; sky bodies at true angular sizes; space close-up in thousands of km; orbit map in true AU with enlarged markers.
creative_direction.opening_hook: A planet just rose out of the sea. Your harbor is draining.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: At 21.2 s the flood is not the worst of it: the rogue pulls the Moon away from Earth for good, shown as the Moon crossing in front of the giant while its distance from Earth climbs.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: It never touched us: it took our Moon and moved our planet onto a Mars-like orbit with five-week-longer northern winters.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The orbit map ends on the rogue's path leaving across the stars; the loop restarts on the same planet rising behind the lighthouse.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the city street, ocean, sailboats, humanoids, Moon, Earth globe, Mars-like planet, sea ice, snowfall and starfield; build a reusable gas giant, a harbour basin kit and an orbit map, and keep the flood choreography story-local.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original procedural score: a low tidal drone and sub pulses under the planet-rise, a held breath before the flood, glassy celestial tones as the Moon is pulled away, thinning night chords, cold winter pads and a wide orbital swell that resolves on the final line.
audio.sfx_direction: Harbour dusk ambience (lapping, ropes, gulls), time-lapse clock ticks, draining gurgle and hull creaks, a rising water roar, 0.3 s silence before the quay is overtopped, then staggered impacts 120-160 ms apart (water slam, boat hulls, a floating car, lamps shorting out), night-to-night whooshes, winter wind and ice creaks, and a deep whoosh into space.

captions.style: Inter Bold uppercase impact phrases with dark outline and shadow, 2-4 words, max two balanced lines

captions.highlights_policy: The physical consequence of each scene in accent colour; at most two emphasis phrases per scene.

Everything drops out for the held breath before the sea overtops the quay.
Water slams over the quay edge with spray.
The lifted yacht slams against the quay edge.

A car lifts and bumps a lamp post.
First lamp shorts out.
Second lamp shorts out.
Third lamp shorts out.
